reading.passage: Most people lose sleep without noticing how little they get. Yet the brain is very busy during the night. Facts learned during the day are moved out of temporary storage and into systems that last longer. In experiments, those who slept after a lesson remembered the material far better than those who stayed awake for the same number of hours. Deep sleep seems to repeat the electrical patterns made earlier in the day, and this repeat strengthens the links between nerve cells. The brain also uses the night to clear waste from its tissues, which may explain why people who lack sleep feel dull and slow. The good news is that one night of real sleep can restore most of what was lost. Bad news: a lost hour of sleep is harder to notice than it sounds, and students who study late often fail to see how far their memory has fallen.

reading.passage: As the population grows older, many countries now face the same question: how can older workers stay useful without wearing themselves out? In one country, a new answer has spread. Firms give workers over sixty a choice between a lighter job with the same pay and a shorter week with the same total pay. The point is not to push people out. It is to let them choose the shape of their later years. Studies show that workers who keep a job after retirement age stay healthier and report more daily satisfaction. Yet the arrangement works only when the job itself is planned again. A tired back, a long meeting, or a night shift can not simply be given to an older person and called flexibility. Several companies have found that the real gain comes from changes that help all workers, such as better lighting and shorter standing tasks. Age, in this view, is not a barrier but a variable that a workplace can design around.

reading.passage: In a small theater, a play is often built without a single famous player. The work begins with a reading, when the director reads the whole script aloud and the company listens. Nothing is decided yet. Then a table is pushed to one side and the players stand up and begin to try things. A line is dropped, a gesture is changed, and the same page is read again. This stage is called the table work, and its only rule is that nothing is perfect for long. The company also keeps two plans on the floor at all times. One follows the written text closely, and the other is free to break it when a better moment appears. Directors often say the second plan is where the play really lives. In the end the audience sees a story that looks inevitable, although nothing about it ever was. The polish comes not from a grand plan but from hundreds of tiny choices made in a quiet room.

reading.passage: A third of the food produced in the world is never eaten. Some of it is lost on the farm or in a truck, but most is thrown away in shops and homes after it looks old. The waste is not only food. Water, land, and fuel have already been used to grow it. Many cities have learned that the cheapest way to help hungry people is not to grow more, but to move what is already there. In several towns, drivers collect bread, fruit, and vegetables that stores can no longer sell. A law of 2016 in one country forced large stores to give away food that they could no longer sell. Critics complained about cost and safety, but the amount rescued soon grew larger than the first results suggested. Many people argue that the habit has changed more than the amount. People who once checked a date and threw the food away now ask who could still eat it. The system is still small, and many countries have no rule at all.

reading.topic: 科技｜太空碎片與連鎖效應
reading.passage: Every object sent into space carries a piece of it, even the paint on its outside. That paint is hit by tiny grains of dust and by the sharp edges of dead machines. Over years, the surface slowly breaks into smaller and smaller pieces, a chain effect that grows step by step. Once a fragment is small enough, it can stay in orbit for a very long time. A paint chip the size of a grain of rice can travel around the earth many times a day. The danger is not the falling object, which usually burns up long before it lands, but the working satellites. A single fast piece can damage a solar panel or stop a signal. Because the number of pieces is growing, engineers now test how to lower a satellite after its work is done, so it can burn safely in a lower layer of air. Several companies also collect old machines that still fly. The task is slow, and each move costs money, but the sky above us is a room that all countries share.

D. Because paint is softer than metal.
option_texts: Because the air high above the earth pushes it upward.

Because the sun pulls it toward the earth.
Because paint is softer than metal.
